"""Chat-turn role detector (layers.15.mlp.down_proj, component 128).

Qwen's chat template opens every turn with "<|im_start|>" followed by a role
word. This component reacts to that role word, and only when the turn opens
after an earlier turn has closed ("<|im_end|>" newline "<|im_start|>"):
  - "assistant" opening the model's reply: strong, about 7.8
  - "user" opening a user turn:             moderate, about 2.6
A fresh "<|im_start|>" right after "<|endoftext|>" (a new packed document)
stays quiet. Everywhere else the component sits near -0.04, with a spread of
about 0.4 that no short rule captures, so the program predicts -0.04 there.
"""

READS = ()

ROLE_ACTIVATION = {"assistant": 7.8, "user": 2.6}
ELSEWHERE = -0.04


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    s = prefix.token_strings
    d = prefix.document_ids
    t = prefix.position
    value = ELSEWHERE
    if t >= 3 and s[t] in ROLE_ACTIVATION and s[t - 1] == "<|im_start|>":
        same_doc = d[t - 3] == d[t] and d[t - 2] == d[t] and d[t - 1] == d[t]
        if same_doc and s[t - 2] == "\n" and s[t - 3] == "<|im_end|>":
            value = ROLE_ACTIVATION[s[t]]
    return carry, float(value)

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 129: a weak, mostly token-level signal.

Plain-terms summary, from ~4M training tokens:
- It goes negative on words about counting and quantities used as abstract
  terms: "count", "number", "num", "probability", "frequency", "integer",
  "coefficient". Mean about -0.44, with large dips (to about -12).
  Its output direction is the opposite: a negative activation raises the
  logits of count/quantity tokens ("counts", "_count", "quantity") as the
  next token.
- It is slightly positive on digits (mean +0.05), and near +0.03 elsewhere.
  Most ordinary tokens have a spread of about +/-0.4 that no rule over the
  prefix explains: token identity, bigrams and recent-count-word context
  together explain only about 3% of the variance.

The program predicts the class mean for each token from a lexicon of
counting words, digits, and everything else. Its variance explained on eval
is about 0.005; a bigger token table would add only a little more.
"""
import re

READS = ()

COUNTING = re.compile(r"count|number|\bnum|probab|frequen|integer|coeff|quantit", re.I)
DIGIT = re.compile(r"\d")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if COUNTING.search(tok):
        value = -0.44
    elif DIGIT.search(tok):
        value = 0.05
    else:
        value = 0.03
    return carry, value

"""Baseline for layers.15.mlp.down_proj component 131.

This component reads one MLP hidden unit of layer 15 (neuron 131 carries ~72% of its
direction) and writes a small signal back into the residual stream. Its activation is
diffuse: typically within about +/-0.5, with rare negative spikes down to about -8 in
English prose and bright positives in code. Neither the current token, the previous
token, the bigram, the character class of the token, the position in the document, nor
the genre of the surrounding text predicts it (each explains about 1% or less of the
variance on held-out tokens).

So the readable program predicts the component's typical value everywhere: its mean,
about 0.025. That explains essentially none of the variance; it is the honest baseline.
"""

READS = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = 0.0254


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """Predict the component's activation at the newest position: a constant."""
    return carry, MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 132: a weak, diffuse feature.

Its activation is the MLP hidden vector dotted with one fixed direction, scaled by the
component's output norm. That direction is spread over thousands of hidden units, and
its variance is driven by context rather than by any token class. This program keeps
only the two effects that are visible in the data:

- the second token of a document (position 1 after a document starts) is often
  positive, about +0.17 on average;
- a token that already occurred earlier in the same document is slightly positive,
  about +0.03 on average, and other tokens sit near 0.

Everything else (the large, sign-flipping excursions) is not captured.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

SECOND_TOKEN = 0.17
REPEATED_TOKEN = 0.03


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    # carry: (document label, tokens seen so far in this document, position in document)
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        seen, pos = set(), 0
    else:
        seen, pos = carry[1], carry[2] + 1
    token = prefix.token_ids[-1]
    repeated = token in seen
    seen.add(token)
    if pos == 1:
        value = SECOND_TOKEN
    elif repeated:
        value = REPEATED_TOKEN
    else:
        value = 0.0
    return (doc, seen, pos), value

"""Layer 15 MLP, hidden unit 133 readout (component down_proj:133).

This component is almost entirely the MLP hidden unit 133 of layer 15 (about 42% of its
input direction) plus many small diffuse terms. Its activation is noisy and spread out:
no token, position, repetition or bag-of-recent-words feature explains it (a full
token-identity table reaches only ~2% of variance on held-out text).

The one readable regularity found: subject pronouns (He, She, They, I, We) sit higher on
average (mean ~0.16 vs ~0.04 elsewhere). That mean shift is all this program encodes.
It explains essentially none of the variance and barely moves the model's output.
"""

READS = ()

SUBJECT_PRONOUNS = frozenset({"He", "She", "They", "I", "We"})
BASE = 0.04  # typical activation on other tokens
PRONOUN = 0.16  # typical activation on subject pronouns


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip()
    return carry, PRONOUN if word in SUBJECT_PRONOUNS else BASE

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 134: a weak, context-driven feature of Chinese prose.

What it does (plain terms): it is most active on Chinese characters that sit inside a run
of Chinese text, and on the particles and intensifiers that lead into a formal news-style
phrase (的, 等, 也, 都, 非常, 十分, 很是, 进一步, 不断 ...). Its largest values come in
official or news Chinese (e.g. 充分[展现], 予以[肯定], 社区居民[的][赞扬]), where the next
word is often a formulaic praise, achievement or support expression. The enumeration comma
(、) pushes it down; Japanese kana and Korean hangul push it up a little. Most of its
variance is not captured by these simple rules.

The program predicts it from four readable pieces:
  1. Chinese density: if the current token is a Han character, scale by the share of
     Han characters among the previous 16 tokens of the same document.
  2. Particles and intensifiers: a fixed list adds a constant.
  3. Punctuation: 、 subtracts a constant.
  4. Kana and hangul: a small constant.
Document boundaries reset the context, as the model does.
"""

import regex

READS = ()

WINDOW = 16
HAN = regex.compile(r"\p{Han}")
KANA_OR_HANGUL = regex.compile(r"[\p{Hiragana}\p{Katakana}\p{Hangul}]")
PARTICLES = {
    "的", "等", "也", "都", "非常", "十分", "很是", "进一步", "不断", "更加",
    "很", "全面", "广泛", "充分", "大家",
}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """Predict this position's activation from the newest token and the Han density before it."""
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    recent = carry[1] if carry is not None and carry[0] == doc else []
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    is_han = 1.0 if HAN.search(token) else 0.0
    density = sum(recent) / len(recent) if recent else 0.0
    value = 1.1 * is_han * density
    value += 1.1 if token in PARTICLES else 0.0
    value -= 0.5 if token == "、" else 0.0
    value += 0.5 if KANA_OR_HANGUL.search(token) else 0.0
    recent = (recent + [is_han])[-WINDOW:]
    return (doc, recent), float(value)

"""Explains layers.15.mlp.down_proj:135: one rank-one piece of layer 15's MLP output.

Its activation is, almost exactly, MLP hidden unit 135 of layer 15 times the size of that unit's
output column. The unit is near zero on most tokens. It is large on tokens that open a
subscript, a superscript or a bracketed group in mathematical or code notation: "_{" after a
variable (a_{1}), "^{", "/(", "(f" (as in print(f"...")), "[List", '["'. Ordinary words are near 0.
Activations are signed; the largest negative values come from legal citations, which this
program does not model.

This program predicts a fixed typical value for each of about 30 token types and 0 for every
other token. The values are averages over training text. It explains about 9-12% of the
variance. Most of what it misses is context inside a token type (for example, "_{" is about 15
after a variable and about 4 after "sum" or "lim"), which needs the model's own state to predict.
"""

READS = ()

# Subscript and superscript openers.
SUBSCRIPT_OPENERS = {"_{": 10.5, "}_{": 7.6, "^{": 7.2, "^(": 11.6, "{{": 6.4}

# Openers of a call, a group or a list in formulas and code.
GROUP_OPENERS = {
    "/(": 11.9, "(f": 7.5, ")/(": 7.8, "*(": 4.2, "-(": 7.4, "[List": 15.9, '["': 3.7,
    "((": 2.9, " ((": 4.5, "(`": 5.3,
}

# LaTeX commands and display-math delimiters.
LATEX_AND_MATH = {
    " \\\"": 2.9, "left": 3.4, "frac": 2.3, "}{": 2.2, "{\\": 1.9, " $$": 2.9,
    " $": 0.9, "Box": 3.5, " \\(": 2.4,
}

# Weak: punctuation and indentation that often open a group.
WEAK = {":": 0.7, " (": 0.6, ' "': 0.6, "  ": 0.6, " ": 0.2, "{": 0.9}

TABLE = {**SUBSCRIPT_OPENERS, **GROUP_OPENERS, **LATEX_AND_MATH, **WEAK}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """This position's activation: the typical value of the newest token, else 0."""
    return carry, TABLE.get(prefix.token_strings[-1], 0.0)

"""Component layers.15.mlp.down_proj:137 (Qwen3-1.7B).

What it does, as far as anyone can tell: almost nothing. Its causal importance is
~0 on every token of a 10M-token corpus, and switching it off changes the model's
next-token predictions by ~1e-6 nats. Its activation is noisy (std 0.28, range
about -1.7 to 2.5) and carries no token-level pattern: knowing the current token,
the previous token, or the bag of the last few tokens explains under 2% of its
variance on held-out text, and the document's own average explains only ~4%.

The one regularity we found is position in the document. The activation is
essentially 0 on a document's first token, is clearly positive on the next two
tokens (about 0.13 on average), then fades back toward its overall mean (about
0.02) over the next several tokens. This program predicts exactly that schedule:
it counts tokens since the current document began and returns the average
activation for that position. It explains about 0.1% of the variance, so it is
a description of the average shape, not of the component's behaviour per token.
"""

READS = ()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # Position within the current document: resets where the document label changes
    # (and at the start of a row, when carry is None).
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or doc != carry[0]:
        pos = 0
    else:
        pos = carry[1] + 1
    if pos == 0:
        value = 0.0  # a document's first token
    elif pos <= 2:
        value = 0.13  # the two tokens after it: the component's only clear bump
    elif pos <= 5:
        value = 0.06  # fading
    else:
        value = 0.02  # the overall average, about 0.025
    return (doc, pos), value

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 138: a diffuse signal with no simple trigger.

What it is: component 138 reads the layer-15 MLP hidden vector through one input
direction V and writes along one output direction U. Its activation is that read-out
times ||U||. V puts about 11% of its energy on hidden unit 138 and spreads the rest over
many other units. Across training text the activation is roughly symmetric around zero,
with spread 0.26. Switching it off changes the model's next-token predictions by only
about 1e-6 nats per position, so it is essentially unimportant to the output.

What was tried: the activation is not predicted by the current token, the previous
token, bigrams, token classes (punctuation, digits, CJK, code symbols, function words),
position in the document, repeated tokens, or a linear fit on 1000 frequent tokens in a
window of 8 previous tokens (out-of-sample R^2 about 0.02). Its best single correlate is
hidden unit 138 itself (r = 0.34). That unit is also not predicted by tokens, though its
highest mean values come from concessive and contrast openers ("Although", "While",
"though", "since") and its lowest from words like "See", "Please", "Therefore".

So this program predicts the component's mean everywhere. It captures essentially none
of the variance (R^2 near 0). A lookup table of token means would add only about 0.02
out of sample, and a short rule set over token classes about 0.001.
"""

READS = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = -0.0064


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    return carry, MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Layer 15 MLP component 139 (down_proj), predicted as its mean value everywhere.

What the component reads: its input direction is almost exactly layer-15 MLP hidden unit 139
(weight 0.997 on that unit), and that unit carries about half of the component's variance.
So the component is, to a good approximation, that one MLP neuron, scaled by its output norm.

What it does: its activation is mostly small (typically within +/-1 of zero) with a thin
negative tail (about 0.1-0.2% of positions below -3, the lowest near -33). Logit-lensing its
output direction suggests negative values push the next-token distribution toward naming
words ("called", "termed", "known as"), but the model's own probability of such words does not
track the activation (correlation 0.01). The most negative values fall on opening parentheses,
"as"/"or"/"for"/"the" inside comparisons and appositives, and on split UTF-8 bytes; these
token classes do not predict the activation on held-out rows (R^2 about 0 for each).

What this program does: it predicts the component's mean activation (0.0365) at every
position. It explains no variance (variance explained about 0 on eval), and its e2e effect is
the same as switching the component off. No simple readable rule I tested does better.
"""

READS = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = 0.0365  # the component's mean over the eval rows


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    return carry, MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Status-predicate detector for layers.15 MLP unit 140 (down_proj component 140).

The component is one MLP hidden unit's output. It fires on the word that says how a thing
stands or turns out: "works", "passed", "finished", "failed", "happens", "exists",
"is valid", "is correct", "is not true", "ran out". It is strongest when the predicate's
subject is a thing or an event ("it works", "that happens", "the tests pass", "this will
work", "doesn't work") and weaker when a person is the subject. Human activity verbs
("studied", "reviewed", "analyzed") push it slightly negative. Everything else is ~0.
"""

STATUS = set("""work works working worked pass passes passed passing fail fails failed failing
succeed succeeds succeeded complete completes completed finish finishes finished happen happens
happened happening occur occurs occurred exist exists existed appear appears appeared apply
applies applied hold holds held remain remains remained stay stays become becomes became change
changes changed vary varies differ run runs ran go goes went come comes came take takes took fit
fits fixed break breaks broke expire expires expired exceed exceeds exceeded valid invalid correct
incorrect true false fine okay ok ready available applicable possible impossible successful
effective acceptable wrong right broken visible satisfied sufficient necessary feasible
successfully correctly properly deleted activated eligible granted spread helps follows reach
seemed operate relevant hard bad hot constant worth obvious deprecated dismissed increasing growing
cost""".split())
HUMAN_ACTIVITY = set("""investigate investigated study studied review reviewed analyze analyzed
analyse believe believed think thought describe described interpret interpreted treat treated
examine examined consider considered produce produced write wrote read""".split())
THING_SUBJECT = set("it that this which what command tests test everything nothing something".split())
NEGATION = set("not never nt cannot don doesn didn won wont isn no 't".split())
AUXILIARY = set("will would should can could must may is are was be been has have still only also just".split())
HUMAN_SUBJECT = set("he she they i we you who".split())
PARTICLES = set("out through apart as to in with up down off over into on".split())


def word(s):
    return s.strip().lower().replace("’", "'")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    t = prefix.position
    cur = word(prefix.token_strings[-1])
    prev = prev2 = ""
    if t >= 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]:
        prev = word(prefix.token_strings[-2])
    if t >= 2 and prefix.document_ids[-3] == prefix.document_ids[-1]:
        prev2 = word(prefix.token_strings[-3])
    if cur in STATUS:
        if prev in NEGATION:
            return carry, 6.0
        if prev in THING_SUBJECT:
            return carry, 7.0
        if prev in AUXILIARY:
            return carry, 4.0
        if prev in HUMAN_SUBJECT:
            return carry, 1.0
        if prev in {"the", "a", "an", "of", "for", "in", "at", "his", "her", "their", "my", "your"}:
            return carry, 0.0
        return carry, 1.6
    if cur in HUMAN_ACTIVITY:
        return carry, -0.2
    if cur in PARTICLES and (prev in STATUS or prev2 in STATUS):
        return carry, 1.0
    return carry, 0.0

What the component does, as far as I could measure:
- Its activation is dense and two-sided: std about 0.44 over all tokens, with

So the program predicts 0 everywhere. Its effect on the model's output is the

against zero_kl 2.29e-6), and its variance explained is about 0.
"""

"""
Predicts layers.15.mlp.down_proj:142, a diffuse feature with no sharp trigger.
Plain-terms idea: it runs higher on words that leave a phrase open (determiners
and articles such as "a", auxiliaries and modals such as "have", "can", "would",
verbs and adjectives) and lower on nouns, numbers, code, whitespace and
punctuation. Its prediction is 0 on a document's first token. Otherwise it is
0.6 x (this token's word-class score) + 2.1 x (a decaying average of the
word-class scores earlier in the same document) - 0.5. The average term is what
makes text with many open-phrase words (ordinary English prose, short captions)
score higher than lists, code or number-heavy text. It explains about 8% of the
variance; the word-class scores are rough hand-set values, not fitted per token.
"""

import regex
import wordnet

READS = ()

DETERMINERS_AUX = set(
    "a an the this that these those their his her its our my your every each some any "
    "all both no one have has had having can could will would shall should may might "
    "must do does did is are was were be been being am not".split()
)
PREPOSITIONS = set("of to in on at by from with for as about into over under".split())
CONJUNCTIONS = set("and or but so because if than".split())
PRONOUNS = set("it he she they we you i me him them us".split())

DECAY = 0.995  # running average over roughly the last 200 tokens of the document


def word_class_score(token):
    """How strongly a token's word class leaves a phrase open (about 0 to 1.5)."""
    w = token.strip()
    if not w:
        return -0.2
    if regex.fullmatch(r"\p{Han}+", w):
        return 1.5
    if regex.fullmatch(r"\p{L}+", w):
        lw = w.lower()
        if lw in DETERMINERS_AUX:
            return 1.5
        if lw in PREPOSITIONS:
            return 0.6
        if lw in CONJUNCTIONS:
            return 0.0
        if lw in PRONOUNS:
            return 0.4
        parts = wordnet.parts_of_speech(lw)
        if parts and "noun" not in parts and ("verb" in parts or "adjective" in parts):
            return 1.3
        if parts == {"noun"}:
            return 0.5
        return 0.8 if parts else 0.4
    if regex.fullmatch(r"\d+", w):
        return -0.1
    if regex.fullmatch(r"\p{P}+|\p{S}+", w):
        return 0.0
    return 0.1


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        running = 0.0  # a new document starts: nothing before it
        first = True
    else:
        running, first = carry[1], False
    value = 0.0 if first else 0.6 * word_class_score(token) + 2.1 * running - 0.5
    # the running average is updated with this token's class score for the next position
    new_running = DECAY * running + (1 - DECAY) * word_class_score(token)
    return (doc, new_running), value

"""Predict the component's typical activation: a constant, about its mean (0.01).

Component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:143 (layer 15 MLP down projection) is
essentially inert. Its causal importance is ~0 at every token (it never passes 0.1 in a
10M-token corpus), and switching it off changes the model's next-token output by ~1e-6 nats.
Its activation is (hidden unit mix) . V, scaled by ||U||: it is roughly zero-mean noise with
std ~0.3, and nothing simple predicts it. The current token explains under 1% of its
variance, the previous few tokens do not help, and position in a document only matters at
the very first token (where it is ~0). So the best simple description is its mean.
"""

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = 0.01  # its mean over eval rows is 0.0094; over training rows about 0.016


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    return carry, MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 144: a negative "an object is coming" signal.

The activation is mostly near zero. It goes clearly negative where the model is about to
need a direct object or a complement:

- a verb that takes an object, e.g. "you can [use] it", "need to [install] the",
  "[add] them": about -0.55 after to / can / will / you / we / I / and / then / by / please,
  and -0.18 after other words. A verb right after a determiner ("the use") is a noun, so 0.
- the "of" of a partitive or quantity phrase, e.g. "some [of] them", "the sum [of]",
  "percent [of]": about -1.5. Any other "of": about -1.0. "kind of", "instead of",
  "because of" are idioms and stay at 0.

It is slightly positive on the light verb "make" (make sure, make use of, +0.5) and on
prepositions such as "to", "for", "with", "through", "across" (+0.2).

WordNet decides which words are verbs. The values are rounded from a least-squares fit on
training rows, and the rule uses only the current token and the one before it.
"""

from functools import lru_cache

import wordnet

READS = ()

# Words after which a bare verb is an instruction or a modal infinitive.
BARE_AFTER = {"to", "can", "will", "should", "must", "would", "could", "may", "might",
              "you", "we", "i", "they", "and", "or", "then", "please", "let", "not", "also", ","}
# Determiners and quantifiers: a verb-shaped word after them is a noun ("the use").
DETERMINERS = {"the", "a", "an", "this", "that", "my", "your", "his", "her", "its", "our",
               "their", "some", "any", "each", "every", "these", "those"}
# Verbs that take no concrete object, so they are not counted as action verbs.
LIGHT_VERBS = {"be", "is", "are", "was", "were", "have", "has", "do", "does", "get", "let",
               "keep", "make", "makes", "made", "making"}
# "of" after a quantity or part word ("some of", "sum of", "percent of") is strongly negative.
QUANTITY_BEFORE_OF = {"some", "most", "all", "many", "each", "both", "none", "any", "two",
                      "three", "four", "five", "several", "few", "half", "one", "more",
                      "percent", "percentage", "majority", "sum", "number", "effect",
                      "combination", "proportion", "fraction", "best"}
# Fixed "of" phrases ("kind of", "instead of") are near zero.
IDIOM_BEFORE_OF = {"kind", "kinds", "type", "sort", "out", "instead", "because", "way",
                   "ways", "capable", "aware", "independent", "regardless", "front"}
PREPOSITIONS = {"to", "for", "with", "on", "in", "from", "at", "through", "across", "via",
                "toward", "towards", "throughout", "beyond", "regarding", "against"}


@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def is_verb(word):
    """WordNet lists this word as a verb in some sense."""
    return word.isalpha() and word.isascii() and "verb" in wordnet.parts_of_speech(word)


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    cur = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    same_doc = len(prefix.document_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip().lower() if same_doc else ""
    if cur == "of":
        if prev in QUANTITY_BEFORE_OF:
            return carry, -1.5
        if prev in IDIOM_BEFORE_OF:
            return carry, 0.0
        return carry, -1.0
    if cur in LIGHT_VERBS:
        return carry, 0.5 if cur.startswith("make") else 0.0
    if is_verb(cur) and prev not in DETERMINERS:
        return carry, -0.55 if prev in BARE_AFTER else -0.18
    if cur in PREPOSITIONS:
        return carry, 0.2
    return carry, 0.0

"""p-82af68dd@100000 layers.15.mlp.down_proj:145: a near-inert component.

What it is: a rank-one piece of layer 15's MLP down projection. Its input direction is
almost entirely MLP hidden unit 145 (about 0.47 of its 0.74 weight norm sits on that one unit,

    " as": -0.55,
    " in": -0.35,

The component reads mostly this one hidden unit of the layer-15 MLP (about 0.82 of its
1.08 norm), with a diffuse remainder. Its activation is mostly small, context-dependent
noise, but it is large on one clear case: a line break that cuts a sentence in two, i.e. a
newline right after a word that cannot end a sentence ("the", "of", "and", "to", "is", ...),
as in "... the probability of the 4-QAM scheme over the<newline>additive white ...". It is
weakly positive on other newlines and on CJK punctuation (、 ，), and slightly negative on
broken or escaped byte fragments (the replacement character, NUL, \\x.., &#).

The program predicts those cases and a small constant elsewhere. It explains about 2.5% of
the variance on eval. A per-token lookup table explains only about 2% out of sample, and
no context feature tried (position, repetition, surprisal, document) does better, so the
rest of the activation is not captured by simple rules.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

FUNCTION_WORDS = frozenset(
    # words that cannot end a sentence: articles, prepositions, conjunctions, auxiliaries
    "a an the this that these those its his her their our my your some any all each every "
    "of to in on at by for from with into over under between through than as "
    "and or but if so because while when which who whom whose what where how "
    "is are was were be been being am not no such other own one "
    "has have had do does did can will would should may might must".split()
)
CJK_PUNCTUATION = frozenset("、，。（）「」！？：；")


def is_newline(token: str) -> bool:
    """A line break token: whitespace holding a newline, or a literal backslash-n."""
    return (token.strip() == "" and ("\n" in token or "\r" in token)) or token == "\\n"


def is_broken(token: str) -> bool:
    """A replacement character, NUL, or an escaped byte or entity fragment."""
    return "�" in token or "\x00" in token or token.startswith(("\\x", "&#"))


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    # the word before this token, if it is in the same document
    ids = prefix.document_ids
    same_document = len(ids) > 1 and ids[-2] == ids[-1]
    before = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip().lower() if same_document else ""
    if is_newline(token):

        return carry, 2.8 if before in FUNCTION_WORDS else 0.15
    if any(ch in CJK_PUNCTUATION for ch in token):
        return carry, 0.45
    if is_broken(token):
        return carry, -0.2
    return carry, -0.03

What the component is: it reads the layer-15 MLP hidden state through a direction (V)
spread thinly over thousands of hidden units, and writes along a direction (U) that is
not a clear token feature. Its activation averages about 0.03 with spread about 0.47, and
switching it off barely changes the model (about 1e-4 nats of loss per token). No concept
I could find explains its activation: token identity, the previous token, position and word
classes together explain well under 1% of its variance on held-out text.

What this program keeps, the only parts with a visible pattern:
- The first token of a row or document gives 0: the component is silent there.
- The second token gives a small positive value (about 0.25 on average).
- Challenge and contrast words push it negative: "why" most strongly (about -1),
  and "what", "how", "but", "however" weakly (about -0.2). Its largest negative values
  come from rhetorical questions in argument and dialogue.
- Every other token sits at the average, about 0.03.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

AVERAGE = 0.03
SECOND_TOKEN = 0.25
CHALLENGE = {"why": -1.0, "what": -0.2, "how": -0.2, "but": -0.2, "however": -0.2}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    # carry: (document id, index of the current token within its document)
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]

        k = 0  # first token of a row or of a document
    else:

"""Explains layers.15.mlp.down_proj:163 (a lexical, spelling-driven feature).

What the component does, in plain terms: its activation is almost entirely a
function of the current token's text, not of its context. It is strongly positive
on a small set of directional/temporal words (over, after, under, lower, below,
above, back, away, off) and on a set of discourse words (Wait, well, will, would,
there, other, ever, never, only). Beyond those words it is a weak spelling pattern:
tokens containing r, l, v or w run positive, and tokens containing c, m, p, s, t,
n, z, q run negative (so "over", "water", "error", "well" are high, while
"to", "in", "at", "an", "that" are low). The first token of each document is ~0.

The program predicts this as a sum of those terms. It explains about 16% of the
variance on held-out text; the rest is context and a long tail of other words,
which a readable rule set does not capture.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# Directional / temporal relation words: the strongest triggers.
SPATIAL = {
    "over", "under", "after", "before", "above", "below",
    "lower", "upper", "back", "away", "off",
}
# Discourse and modal words that also fire it.
DISCOURSE = {
    "wait", "well", "will", "would", "there", "other", "ever", "never", "only",
}

# Spelling weights (per occurrence of the letter in the token).
POSITIVE_LETTERS = "rlvw"
NEGATIVE_LETTERS = "cmpsztnq"
WEAK_NEGATIVE_LETTERS = "ak"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    # The first token of a document (or of the row) has near-zero activation.
    t = prefix.position
    if t == 0 or prefix.document_ids[t] != prefix.document_ids[t - 1]:
        return carry, 0.0

    text = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    word = text.strip().lower()

    value = 0.1  # baseline
    value += 0.49 * sum(word.count(c) for c in POSITIVE_LETTERS)
    value -= 0.22 * sum(word.count(c) for c in NEGATIVE_LETTERS)
    value -= 0.16 * sum(word.count(c) for c in WEAK_NEGATIVE_LETTERS)
    if word in SPATIAL:
        value += 2.6
    if word in DISCOURSE:
        value += 1.5
    if word.isalpha():
        value += 0.19
    return carry, float(value)

What it is: one rank-one piece of the MLP down projection of layer 15. Its activation is a
dense linear readout of the layer's 6144 MLP hidden units (about 16% of its variance comes

What we could find: no token-level or context-level rule predicts it. Token identity, the
previous token, the bigram and the coarse script/category of the token explain essentially
none of its variance on held-out text. Inside repeated text it runs only slightly higher
(about 0.03 to 0.05 on average, against 0.03 elsewhere). Its typical value is about +0.03,
with a heavy tail (rarely up to about 5, rarely down to about -2); its strongest cases have
no clear theme.

The one regularity found is positional: at the very first token of a document the
activation is about 0, over the next ~19 tokens it sits slightly below zero (about -0.06),
and after that it returns to its typical value (about +0.035). This program predicts those
three levels and nothing else, so it explains well under 1% of the variance.
"""

READS = ()

FIRST_TOKEN = 0.0  # position 0 of a document
EARLY = -0.06  # positions 1..19 of a document
LATE = 0.035  # later positions: the component's typical value


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    # carry: (document id, position where this document starts)
    start = carry[1] if carry is not None and carry[0] == doc else prefix.position
    age = prefix.position - start  # tokens since the document began
    if age == 0:
        value = FIRST_TOKEN
    elif age < 20:
        value = EARLY
    else:
        value = LATE

BLOB_VALUE = 8.5  # mean activation over a blob's tokens

    return ch.isascii() and (ch.isalnum() or ch in "+/=")

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj component 182: a diffuse, near-constant component.

What the data show (measured on training rows):
- Its activation is roughly zero-mean noise with std ~0.3 that is not tied to any
  surface feature we can read from the tokens. A lookup of the token's identity,
  token/previous-token tables, byte or character categories, and position buckets
  all explain about 0-1% of its variance on held-out rows.
- At a document's first token (position 0) it is always ~0.
- Its causal importance is essentially zero (CI averages ~3e-7 and never passes 0.1),
  and switching it off changes the model's next-token predictions by ~1e-6 nats.

after the first, and 0 at the first position of each document.
"""

READS = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = 0.02  # average over all positions in the eval rows


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # The first token of a document has no context and its activation is ~0.
    first = prefix.position == 0 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    if first:
        return carry, 0.0
    return carry, MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 183 (component p-82af68dd ... down_proj:183), as a word rule.

What it is: a single MLP hidden unit whose write direction (its down_proj column) pushes
the next-token distribution toward verbs of changing or transforming something ("turn into",
"convert to", "replace", "modify", "transform").

What this program does: it reads only the newest token and the one before it, and gives a
signed guess at the unit's activation (values shrunk toward 0, since the rule is weak):
  - -0.8 on the word right after "Edit" (as in "Edit the file");
  - -0.3 on instruction-style change verbs (edit, adjust, modify, convert, turn, ...);
  - +0.3 on code words for replacing, removing or filtering (replace, remove,
    filtered, eliminate, raise, throw, ...);
  - 0 everywhere else.

It explains almost nothing. The unit's activation is spread thinly over almost every token
(mean |activation| about 0.3). On held-out eval rows this rule gets variance explained of
about 0.0002 (Pearson r about 0.03), and no word list found reached more than about 1% even
with perfect values. Its large values are not reliably tied to any word. The one solid fact
is the output side: its write direction promotes change and transform words (变成/become,
transform, replace, 改为/change to, convert), which is what the signs are loosely about.
"""

READS = ()

CHANGE_VERBS = {
    "edit", "adjust", "modify", "convert", "adapt", "update", "expand", "combine",
    "change", "turn", "make", "add",
}
REPLACE_WORDS = {
    "_replace", "replace", "replacing", "remove", "removed", "filter", "filtered",
    "eliminate", "corrected", "converted", "raise", "throw", "becomes", "into",
}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    same_doc = len(prefix.document_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    before = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip().lower() if same_doc else ""
    if before == "edit":

    if word in CHANGE_VERBS:

What the component is: one rank-one piece of the MLP down projection. It reads the
MLP's hidden vector (6144 units) through one direction, V[:, 184], and writes along
one output direction, U[:, 184]. Its activation is the projection of the hidden vector
onto that direction, times the length of U.

What we found: the activation is roughly symmetric around zero (std about 0.29, mean
about -0.027), and it almost never matters to the model: its causal importance is
near 0 on every token, and switching it off changes the output by about 1e-6 nats.
It does not respond to any token class we could name (letters, digits, punctuation,

on held-out text. The one real structure is that it is autocorrelated over nearby
positions, which comes from the context the MLP sees, not from a rule on the tokens.

So this program does not explain the activation. It predicts the component's typical
value everywhere, which is the best constant for squared error and leaves the model's
output essentially unchanged.
"""

"""Second-token predictor for component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:185.

What the component is: a dense readout of layer 15's MLP hidden state. About 6000 hidden
units contribute to it and none dominates (the largest, unit 185, explains about 12 percent
of its variance). Its activation has mean -0.05 and std 0.28, and it is not explained by
meaning or surface form. Token identity explains about 2 percent of its variance on held-out
text, a 77,000-entry lookup table; character class (letters, digits, CJK, punctuation,
whitespace) explains about 0.1 percent; the previous token explains nothing.

The one regularity that is simple: position within a document. The first token of a
document is near 0, the second averages +0.2, the third +0.04, and the tokens after drift
from about 0 down to -0.05 by position 10 or so. This program predicts those values,
resetting at every document boundary, as the model does. It captures only about a quarter
of a percent of the variance, so it is a faithful but weak description.
"""

READS = ()

MEAN = -0.05  # typical value for tokens deep in a document
FIRST, SECOND, THIRD = 0.0, 0.2, 0.04


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        n = 0  # first token of a new document
    else:
        n = carry[1] + 1
    if n == 0:
        value = FIRST
    elif n == 1:
        value = SECOND
    elif n == 2:
        value = THIRD
    else:
        value = MEAN
    return (doc, n), value

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 186, seen through its down_proj component.

What it does, in plain terms: the component's activation is dominated by one MLP
hidden unit (unit 186 of layer 15) scaled by a fixed weight (correlation about 0.68 with
that unit's value). That unit is mildly
positive at the end of a sentence (". ! 。 ！ ?") and at a few words that open or
carry a customer-facing sentence ("you", "we", "us", "it", "this", "so", "if", "for",
"can", "available", "today", "information", "contact", "more"). It is slightly
negative almost everywhere else, including code and markup. Its strongest values
(10 to 20) sit in promotional web copy, but those are rare, and word identity explains
only a little of its variance.

This program predicts that pattern with group means fitted on training rows:
the first token of a document is 0; sentence-ending punctuation is +0.25; the
customer-facing words are +0.08; everything else is -0.04.

What it gets: a correct sign and rough size on the common cases, and e2e behaviour
close to switching the component off (kl_fraction about 0.98). What it misses: the
large spikes and the diffuse bulk of variance, which need the surrounding context.
A 1000-entry token-by-token lookup table would reach about 0.02 held-out variance
explained; this grouped version reaches about 0.009.
"""

READS = ()

SENTENCE_END = {".", "。", "!", "！", "?", "？"}
CUSTOMER_WORDS = {
    "you", "we", "us", "it", "this", "so", "if", "for", "can",
    "available", "today", "information", "contact", "more",
}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    if prefix.position == 0:
        return carry, 0.0
    raw = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    word = raw.strip().lower()
    if raw.strip() in SENTENCE_END or raw.rstrip("\n") in SENTENCE_END:
        return carry, 0.25
    if word in CUSTOMER_WORDS:
        return carry, 0.08
    return carry, -0.04

"""Layer 15 MLP unit 187 (the down_proj component 187), read as a doc-parameter detector.

The unit is near zero on most text. It goes negative inside source-code documentation,
most strongly on the words that open a documented parameter or return value:
  - Javadoc / JSDoc / PHPDoc tags:  "@param name description", "@return description"
  - Sphinx tags:                    ":param name: ...", ":returns: ..."
  - JSON tool schemas:              "description": "..."
The strongest values fall on the first few words after such a tag and fade by about
the seventh word. A doc-comment opener ("///", triple quotes, "/**") on a line is
moderately negative. Ordinary "//", "#" and "*" comment lines were tried and left at 0,
since they added little variance explained and hurt the model's next-token loss.
Everything else predicts 0.

The program keeps the current line (reset at each newline and at each new document)
and counts the words since a tag on that line.
"""
import re

READS = ()

# A tag that opens a parameter or return description, anywhere on a line.
TAG = re.compile(r"@\s*(param|returns?|throws|exception)\b|:(param|returns?|raises)\b|\"description\":")
# A doc-comment opener at the start of a line.
DOC = re.compile(r"^\s*(///|\"\"\"|/\*\*)")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # A new document starts a fresh line state.
    new_doc = len(prefix.document_ids) < 2 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    if carry is None or new_doc:
        carry = {"line": "", "since_tag": None}
    text = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    line, since = carry["line"], carry["since_tag"]
    if since is not None:
        since += 1
    if "\n" in text:
        # A newline ends the line; the new line starts with whatever follows it.
        line, since = text.rsplit("\n", 1)[1], None
    else:
        line = line + text
    if since is None and TAG.search(line):
        since = 0  # the token just read is the tag's last token
    carry = {"line": line, "since_tag": since}

    if since is not None:
        # Words after a parameter/return tag: strongest at first, fading by the seventh.
        if since < 3:
            value = -7.0
        elif since < 7:
            value = -4.0
        else:
            value = 0.0
    elif DOC.search(line):
        value = -2.5
    else:
        value = 0.0
    return carry, value

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 191 (the component's own index), a weak lexical feature.

The component reads the MLP's hidden unit 191 in layer 15 almost one-for-one: that
unit alone accounts for about a third of its variance. Its activation is weakly
positive on words about choosing and handling objects and items (select, identify,
object(s), item(s), id, inventory, product, buying), and weakly negative on words about
ending or running a command or process (exit, finished, command, termination, HTTP).

This program predicts +0.4 on the positive words, -0.4 on the negative ones, and 0
elsewhere. It explains almost none of the variance (about 0.1%): most of the activation
depends on context that no single token reveals.
"""
from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

POSITIVE = {
    " select", " identify", " object", " objects", " item", " items",
    " id", " inventory", " product", " buying",
}
NEGATIVE = {" exit", " finished", " command", " termination", " HTTP"}
WEIGHT = 0.4


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if token in POSITIVE:
        return carry, WEIGHT
    if token in NEGATIVE:
        return carry, -WEIGHT
    return carry, 0.0
